passage:
Thursday

Dear Diary,
A new boy called Lokesh joined our class today. He walks with crutches. At break everyone stared, and Manav said loudly, "What's wrong with your legs?" Lokesh went red and looked at his shoes.
Mrs. Fernandes heard. She said, "Manav, if you're curious, you can ask Lokesh kindly if he'd like to tell you. And nothing is wrong with him. His body just works in its own way." Then she started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.
Lokesh was really good at it. I didn't talk to him today, and I feel a bit bad about that. Tomorrow I'm saving him a seat at lunch.

Afreen

qa.q: What game did Mrs. Fernandes start?
qa.a: She started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.

qa.q: How does Afreen feel about not talking to Lokesh?
qa.a: Afreen feels a bit guilty about it and plans to make up for it by saving him a seat at lunch.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Fernandes turn the moment around?
qa.a: She showed Manav a kind way to be curious, said difference is not something wrong, and chose a game that included Lokesh.

qa.q: What was it like for Lokesh when Manav asked about his legs?
qa.a: It was embarrassing for him, which is why he went red and looked at his shoes.

grounding: It shows children staring and asking a blunt question about a disabled classmate, and a teacher modelling respectful curiosity and including him.

passage:
The whistle blew for kho-kho in the dusty yard of the village school. Darshan saw Nikita step forward, her hearing aid tucked behind one ear.
"Not you," said one boy. "You won't hear the whistle."
Nikita's hands dropped. She walked back to the neem tree and sat alone.
Darshan felt his stomach twist, but he said nothing.
Master-ji had seen. He crouched beside Nikita and asked, "What would help you play?"
She thought. "If you wave your hand when you blow."
"Good idea." He turned to the others. "From today, whistle and a wave. Nikita's in."
Nikita ran the fastest chase of the afternoon. Later, Darshan sat next to her under the neem tree and asked how she'd thought of the wave.

qa.q: Where did Nikita sit after being told she couldn't play?
qa.a: She sat alone under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when Nikita was left out?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a bit guilty, with his stomach twisting, even though he said nothing.

qa.q: What did Master-ji do that the other children could learn from?
qa.a: He asked Nikita what would help instead of deciding for her, and changed the rule so everyone could play.

qa.q: How did being left out affect Nikita?
qa.a: She felt hurt and shut out, which shows when her hands dropped and she sat alone.

grounding: It shows children leaving a peer with a hearing aid out of play, and a teacher modelling respectful inclusion that others see.

passage: Clara, ten, noticed it on Gabriel's first week at the school in Seville. The new boy used a wheelchair, and at break the others stood in a tight group, staring and whispering. One asked loudly, 'What happened to your legs?' Gabriel went red. Then nobody asked him to play tag. Clara felt uncomfortable, but she didn't know what to do. The next day their teacher, Señora Ruiz, sat with the class. 'It's fine to be curious. Gabriel, would you like to tell us about your chair, or which games you like?' Gabriel shrugged, then grinned. 'I'm really fast on the basketball court.' That break Clara went up to him. 'Want to be on my team?' They lost, but Gabriel scored twice, and the group stopped whispering.

qa.q: What game did Gabriel say he was fast at?
qa.a: Basketball.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling during Gabriel's first week?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and unsure, seeing him stared at and left out but not knowing what to do.

qa.q: What did Señora Ruiz model for the class?
qa.a: Respectful curiosity: asking Gabriel if he wanted to share, and finding games he enjoys, instead of staring or blunt questions.

qa.q: How might Gabriel have felt when asked 'What happened to your legs?'
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and singled out, going red in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child noticing classmates staring at and excluding a disabled peer, and a teacher modelling respectful curiosity and inclusion.

passage: In the Class 4 art room, Usha Ma'am heard the whisper behind her. 'Why does Wasim have that thing in his ear? Is he deaf?' Two boys giggled. Wasim, nine, lowered his head and pretended to colour. Usha felt a flash of anger, then took a breath. She didn't scold the boys in front of everyone. She sat at their table. 'Good question, but let's ask kindly. Wasim, would you like to tell us about your hearing aid, or would you rather not?' Wasim hesitated, then held it up. 'It makes sounds louder. I can hear you better with it.' 'That's clever,' said one boy. Usha nodded. 'Different bodies need different tools.' At the end of the lesson she asked Wasim to hand out the paints, and the boys chatted with him as he did.

qa.q: What did Wasim do when the boys giggled?
qa.a: He lowered his head and pretended to colour.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she heard the whisper?
qa.a: She felt a flash of anger, then calmed herself before responding.

qa.q: Why did Usha give Wasim the choice to share or not?
qa.a: It respected his privacy and dignity while showing the class how to ask kindly.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt holding up his hearing aid?
qa.a: He was probably nervous at first, then relieved when the boy said it was clever.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing children's blunt questions about a disabled peer and modelling respectful curiosity and inclusion.

passage: I'm Kiran, and I was in Pallavi's class the year she came back after her operation. She walked with crutches, slowly. At lunch, a few girls said she'd slow them down in hopscotch, and they just started without her. Pallavi sat on the step, watching, pretending she didn't mind. I don't know exactly what she was feeling. But she didn't eat her lunch. The next day our class teacher, Mr Dsilva, asked us all to invent a new game where everyone could play, sitting or standing. Pallavi came up with one using a ball and chalk circles. We played it all term. I remember thinking I should have done something myself, the first day. I didn't. I'm still a bit ashamed about that.

qa.q: What did Pallavi use to walk?
qa.a: Crutches.

qa.q: What does Kiran feel looking back on the first day?
qa.a: Kiran feels a bit ashamed about not doing something to include Pallavi.

qa.q: What did Mr Dsilva do to model inclusion?
qa.a: He asked the class to invent a game everyone could play, which let Pallavi join and lead.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt sitting on the step?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and hurt, even though she pretended not to mind.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's account, children leaving out a disabled peer and a teacher modelling inclusion so that difference is not seen as a flaw.

passage:
Monday: A new girl, Kalyani, wheeled into Class 5. Pankaj stared at her chair with its shiny rims and heard Vikram mutter, "She can't play kho-kho, so don't pick her." Pankaj said nothing, his face going warm.
Wednesday: Mrs Rao, their teacher, had noticed. In class she said, "Kalyani, would you tell us about your chair, if you like?" Kalyani grinned and showed them the brakes. Pankaj asked how fast it went. "Faster than you downhill," she said, and everyone laughed.
Friday: At break Pankaj and Kalyani invented a relay where she carried the baton round the track on her chair. Vikram asked to join. Pankaj felt proud, but he also thought about Monday, when he had kept quiet.

qa.q: What did Kalyani show the class on Wednesday?
qa.a: She showed them the brakes on her chair.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling on Monday when Vikram muttered about Kalyani?
qa.a: Pankaj felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, his face going warm, but he stayed silent.

qa.q: How did Mrs Rao help the class?
qa.a: She modelled respectful curiosity by inviting Kalyani to share only if she wanted, which turned staring into friendly questions.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have experienced her first week?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out on Monday, then more welcome once classmates asked real questions and played with her.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching children stare at and exclude a disabled peer, and a teacher modelling respectful curiosity that leads to inclusion.
